overview: This event turns the spin family into distinct problems instead of one big emergency blob. You should be ready to brief a clean erect spin entry and recovery, recognize when an inverted or progressive spin is actually developing, and then switch gears to accelerated-stall cues and a disciplined AOA approach picture.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: The intentional erect spin teaches you how a fully stalled, yaw-driven departure is entered, recognized, and recovered before altitude discipline becomes the real emergency. The point is not to be dramatic; it is to make the recovery inputs feel procedural instead of surprising.

children.text: Trim the aircraft for about 150 KIAS in straight-and-level flight, complete PSSA, clear the area, and do not enter below 13,500 feet AGL.
The overall event guardrails still matter: enter below 22,000 feet PA and be recovered above 10,000 feet PA.
Retard PCL to IDLE first, then raise the nose to about 30 degrees nose high.
At the first stick shaker, add slight rudder in the desired spin direction.
At the full stall and nose drop, apply full rudder in the direction of rotation, full aft stick, and keep the ailerons neutral.
Call out altitude, AOA, airspeed, and turn-needle indications so you stay ahead of what the aircraft is doing.
Recover with the published Inadvertent Departure from Controlled Flight procedure rather than trying to create a private spin technique.
Once the rotation stops, neutralize the rudder and recover from the resulting unusual attitude without pulling so aggressively that you create a secondary stall.
After recovery, check and report oil pressure before you add power back in.

Common misses are raising the nose before PCL is at IDLE, letting external fixation delay the recovery, forgetting to neutralize controls as the rotation stops, or pulling too hard in the recovery and stalling it again.
Ailerons stay neutral in the spin, and aft stick held at the wrong time can delay recovery.

items.text: Intentional inverted spins are prohibited. You still need to understand them because a poorly managed inverted departure can flatten into an unusual picture that looks very different from an erect spin.

children.text: The usual setup is a high-pitch, high-power, low-airspeed mistake: roughly 60 to 90 degrees nose high, PCL at MAX, and around 50 KIAS before the aircraft rolls and departs.
Torque and aft-CG effects drive the departure more than the clean yaw entry picture you use for an erect spin.
Expect a flatter spin than the erect case, often around 30 degrees nose low with slight pitch oscillations.
Airspeed is typically around 40 KIAS, AOA trends toward 0 units, and the G cue is negative, around minus 1.5 G.
If the nose is steeply down and the airspeed is rapidly increasing, you may actually be looking at an inverted spiral instead.
An early reduction of PCL to IDLE is the first high-value move because power helps sustain the inverted spin.
With PCL at IDLE and ailerons neutral, some incipient inverted departures will transition out of the spin or become an inverted spiral that you then sort out with the published OCF logic.
Do not confuse a steep, accelerating inverted spiral with the flatter low-airspeed inverted spin picture.
Leaving power at MAX is exactly how you keep the inverted spin going.
Speed-brake position is not the magic answer here; it is not what decides whether the departure develops or recovers.

items.text: A progressive spin is not a new maneuver. It is what you create by applying the wrong recovery inputs to a steady-state spin, which is why this brief is really about avoiding self-inflicted escalation.

children.text: The classic cause is reversing rudder while still holding full aft stick during a steady-state spin recovery attempt.
That combination drops the nose, keeps the aircraft rotating in the original direction for roughly 1.5 to 2 more turns, and drives the airspeed up hard.
Airspeed can build as high as about 175 KIAS while the aircraft is still rotating, which is one reason the sight picture feels worse than a normal spin.
If the wrong rudder and aft stick are held long enough, the aircraft can settle into a steady-state spin in the opposite direction.
Do not try to invent a special progressive-spin technique. Go back to the published OCF/departure recovery procedure and stop the control-input mistake that caused the problem.
The real prevention is procedural discipline: identify the direction of rotation, apply the correct rudder logic once, and do not reverse it because the airplane feels wrong.

items.text: An accelerated stall is a stall driven by excessive AOA under load, not by slow indicated airspeed alone. It is the trap that catches pilots who think a fast airplane cannot still be stalled if they are pulling hard enough.

children.text: The event emphasis is the approach-turn and abrupt-pull environment, but the core lesson is broader: a wing stalls whenever you demand more lift than it can produce.
Higher bank angle means higher load factor, which means higher stall speed and less margin if you keep pulling.
Expect more pronounced buffet once you get above about 2 G, with especially heavy buffet above about 3 G.
The break is often an abrupt lateral roll-off rather than a gentle nose-drop warning.
At 90 degrees of bank the lift requirement becomes impossible, which is why the aircraft simply falls if you try to hold it there.
Reduce AOA first by easing the back-stick and unloading the wing.
Reduce bank angle as required, then rebuild airspeed instead of trying to hold the same turn and make the buffet go away.
Do not sustain heavy buffet in an attempt to salvage the maneuver; that only adds overstress risk.
The common mental trap is focusing on IAS and ignoring that a hard pull at 200 KIAS can still exceed critical AOA.
This is one more reason nose-low unusual-attitude recoveries must stay smooth. An aggressive pull can turn the recovery itself into the stall.

items.text: The AOA approach teaches you to fly the aircraft at the optimum on-speed condition instead of chasing one fixed airspeed. The scan is simple on purpose: keep the aircraft at about 10.5 units AOA, control rate of descent with power, and still transition to a normal flared landing.

children.text: After a touch-and-go, climb out at 120 KIAS with flaps up and return to pattern altitude.
On downwind, reduce power to about 15 to 20 percent, configure as briefed, and transition to the amber-donut on-speed picture.
Approximate on-speed references are about 110 KIAS flaps up, 100 KIAS flaps TO, and 95 KIAS flaps LDG, but the real target is 10 to 11 units AOA regardless of weight or flap setting.
Once on speed, use about 25 to 30 percent power to hold pattern altitude and keep 3/4 to 1 wingtip spacing on downwind.
Complete the Before Landing Checklist before abeam.
At the 180, reduce power back toward 15 to 20 percent, lower the nose slightly to hold 10.5 units, and start the turn.
Expect less bank than a normal pattern, especially with TO or LDG flaps, so you do not tighten the turn unnecessarily.
At the 90, the target is still 10.5 units and about 450 feet AGL.
On final, scan the AOA indexer, aim point, and altimeter together. Use pitch to keep the donut and power to manage the glidepath.
When established with about 1200 to 1500 feet of straightaway remaining, you want about 200 feet AGL and 10.5 units until you are beyond the runway numbers.
This is still an AOA approach to a normal flared landing, not an AOA arrival all the way onto the runway. Expect to add power during the flare transition as the nose lowers.
Flaps-up AOA approaches are difficult and can create high descent rates at low power, so flaps LDG is preferred and flaps TO is only a compromise.
The biggest misses are over-correcting nose attitude, forgetting that power changes affect the AOA picture, using normal-pattern bank angles, and failing to transition to a normal flare.

studyNotes.summary: Keep the spin branches separate in your head, then brief the accelerated-stall and AOA patterns with the same level of discipline.

summary: Spin-family recovery logic, accelerated-stall cues, and AOA approach technique.
title: Spins and AOA Approaches
